explanations.explanation: That's the picture, baker. The singer says, "As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master…" (Psalm 123:2). Think of a busy kitchen where everybody's eyes are on the one hand that's about to point. Nobody's looking at their shoes. Everybody's looking at that hand.

Soldiers watching for a signal is a good picture, and I can see why you picked it. But the singer doesn't use it. He says, "As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master…" (Psalm 123:2). These are servants, friend, not soldiers, and their eyes are on a master's hand.

explanations.answer: Farmers watching the sky for rain
explanations.explanation: Farmers and rain make a fine picture, and plenty of people have looked up that way. This singer doesn't, though. He says, "As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master…" (Psalm 123:2). The eyes aren't on the sky, baker. They're on a hand.

True! The singer doubles it up: "…as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress…" (Psalm 123:2). That's a second servant with her eyes on a second hand. Two pictures, one idea: these eyes stay locked in, and they aren't wandering off for a snack break.

It's actually true, friend. The singer gives a second picture right after the first: "…as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress…" (Psalm 123:2). So that's a servant and a maidservant, a master and a mistress. Both of them are watching a hand.
That's right. The verse says their eyes are on the LORD their God "…until He shows us mercy." (Psalm 123:2). There's no timer on this one, baker. They keep looking until the mercy comes.

Waiting for the morning is a real kind of waiting, and I see why you picked it. But this singer doesn't say that. He says their eyes are on the LORD "…until He shows us mercy." (Psalm 123:2). The wait ends with mercy, friend, not with the sunrise.

I get why you'd pick that, since the next verses talk about scorn. But the singer never says they're waiting for anyone to leave. Their eyes are on the LORD "…until He shows us mercy." (Psalm 123:2). Their waiting is tied to Him, baker, not to what the scorners do.

Contempt is right, baker. The singer says, "Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy, for we have endured much contempt." (Psalm 123:3). The next verse says it comes "…from the arrogant…" and "…from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). Being looked down on like that is heavy, and I think that's why the asking is so loud.

Hunger is a real hardship, but it isn't what this singer names. He says they have "…endured much contempt." (Psalm 123:3). The pain here is being looked down on by the arrogant and the proud, friend. Nobody mentions an empty stomach.

Sickness is a heavy thing to carry, but that's not what's in this verse. The singer says, "…for we have endured much contempt." (Psalm 123:3). The next verse adds that it's "…from the arrogant…" and "…from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). So the trouble comes from people, baker, not from a bug going around.

Not quite, friend. The psalm ends right in the middle of the asking, with "We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). There's no answer in these verses and no word that the scorn has stopped. The song just stops with the waiting still going.

Right, baker. Psalm 123 closes with "We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). These verses show no answer from the LORD, and they never say the scorn stopped. The song ends on the asking.

Israel is right! David says, "If the LORD had not been on our side—let Israel now declare—" (Psalm 124:1). He's calling the whole nation to say it out loud together. That's a lot of voices for one sentence, baker.
Egypt is a big name in the Bible, but it's not in this line. David says, "…let Israel now declare…" (Psalm 124:1). The ones called to declare are Israel, friend, not Egypt.
Babylon shows up in a lot of the Bible, but not here. David says, "…let Israel now declare…" (Psalm 124:1). It's Israel's song to sing, baker, and Babylon isn't part of it.

True! David says that without the LORD on their side, "…they would have swallowed us alive…" (Psalm 124:3). He says it right after "…when their anger flared against us…" (Psalm 124:3). Notice it's a what-if, baker. He's telling you what would have happened without the LORD on their side, and it's a scary picture.

It's true, friend. David says, "…when their anger flared against us, then they would have swallowed us alive…" (Psalm 124:3). That's the what-if if the LORD had not been on their side. It's a scary picture, but it's the one David paints.

Careful, baker, this one's a what-if. David says "…the raging waters would have swept us away." (Psalm 124:5). Would have, not did. The floods were only the picture of what could have happened without the LORD on their side.

Right, baker. Every flood line in this psalm is a "would have," like "…then the floods would have engulfed us… then the raging waters would have swept us away." (Psalm 124:4-5). David is telling what would have happened if the LORD had not been on their side (Psalm 124:1). Then he blesses the LORD, who "…has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6).

explanations.answer: Give them as prey to their teeth
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6). Notice what he's thankful for, something that didn't happen. That's a funny kind of gift, and it's a real one.

explanations.answer: Hand them as spoil to their swords
explanations.explanation: Swords and spoil sound like a good fit, but that's not the line. David says the LORD "…has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6). Teeth, friend, not swords. David is blessing the LORD for what He didn't do.

explanations.answer: Leave them as chaff for the wind
explanations.explanation: Chaff in the wind is a vivid picture, but it's not this one. David says the LORD "…has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6). So it's teeth, baker. Nobody's getting blown around in this verse.

explanations.answer: A bird from the fowler's snare
explanations.explanation: A bird from the snare, that's right! David says, "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler…" (Psalm 124:7). A fowler is someone who traps birds. So the picture is a bird slipping out of the trapper's snare.

explanations.answer: A deer from the hunter's bow
explanations.explanation: A deer is a good picture, but it's not David's. He says, "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler…" (Psalm 124:7). A fowler is a bird catcher, friend. So the one getting away is a bird, not a deer.

explanations.answer: A lamb from the lion's mouth
explanations.explanation: That's a dramatic one, baker, but David doesn't say it here. He says, "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler…" (Psalm 124:7). A fowler catches birds, so a bird is the one slipping away. No lions in this verse.
True! David says, "the net is torn, and we have slipped away." (Psalm 124:7). The trap is ripped, and the bird is out. That's one busted net, baker.
It's true, friend. David says, "the net is torn, and we have slipped away." (Psalm 124:7). The trap didn't hold, so the bird slipped out. A torn net is the whole point of the picture.

explanations.answer: In the name of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. David ends with, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). After all those floods and nets, he lands on one place for help. It's a good way to end a song.

Walls feel like help, and I see why you'd pick them. But David doesn't say that. He says, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). Walls don't get a mention, friend. The help is in the LORD's name.

explanations.answer: In the strength of their king
explanations.explanation: Strength in a king is a fair guess, friend. But David points somewhere else. He says, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). The help is in the LORD's name, baker, not in a king.
True! The last line reads, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). Maker of heaven and earth, baker. Everything else in the song gets small next to that.

It's true, friend. David finishes with, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). That's how the song closes. The One they call on for help is the One who made heaven and earth.
